After the Revolution New England emptied northward.
Farms in Connecticut and central Massachusetts had been divided among sons for four generations and the soil was worn,
and the war had shown thousands of men the country beyond.
Vermont, a state from 1791, and the northern and western counties of New York filled with Yankee families.
The Hutchinses went in stages. Thomas and Priscilla were at Winchester, New Hampshire,
by 1771; in 1777 Thomas bought land at Weathersfield, on the Connecticut River in Vermont,
and in 1792 their daughter Jane was born there; Cyrel’s son Dana was born in Vermont in 1795,
and Cyrel’s parents, Thomas and Priscilla, died at Saint Albans, near Lake Champlain,
in 1810. Cyrel and Betsey went on into Franklin County, New York — in 1808 by one account,
during or just after the War of 1812 by another — crossing Lake Champlain on the ice with their children,
the horses’ hoofs wrapped in sacking so they would not slip.
They farmed at Constable, on the Canadian border, where Cyrel and his sons built a tavern.
The town is named for William Constable, a partner in the Macomb Purchase of 1791,
which bought most of northern New York and sold it off as farms.
The War of 1812 was fought along that border: the American army wintered at French Mills in 1813 to 14,
and the village was renamed Fort Covington for General Leonard Covington, mortally wounded at Crysler’s Farm.
